content.intro: Node.js Benchmarking and Runtime Experiments is part of specialized topics and continued learning. This lesson connects Reproducible experiments, Benchmark design, The built-in benchmark runner where supported to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Performance work starts with a representative measurement and a profile, not with guesswork or isolated microbenchmarks. Record a baseline, repeat the workload, report runtime/version and variance, and compare correctness as well as speed.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Performance work starts with a representative measurement and a profile, not with guesswork or isolated microbenchmarks. Measure latency, throughput, event-loop delay, CPU, and memory under representative workloads before optimizing.

items.title: Reproducible experiments
items.text: For Reproducible experiments, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Benchmark design
items.text: Measure a representative workload, repeat runs, record runtime/configuration, and use a profiler before optimizing. One microbenchmark is not a universal result.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Node.js Benchmarking and Runtime Experiments. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Reproducible experiments; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Benchmark design, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Optimizing before measuring or treating a single benchmark run as a universal conclusion.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Use reproducible workloads, profiler evidence, multiple runs, and regression thresholds.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
